name: Asiel
title: Simeonite patriarch mentioned in the Books of Chronicles
summary: Asiel is one of the prominent ancestors in the tribe of Simeon, known from the genealogy in 1 Chronicles (1 Chron 4:35), where he appears in the line Asiel → Seraja → Josibja → Jehu. Although there is no independent account of his life, his significance emerges through his descendants, who belonged to the leading Simeonite heads. During the reign of King Hezekiah (ca. 715–686 BC), these leaders set out to seek new grazing lands and expanded the territory of the Simeonites by going to the area near Gedor, where they drove out the Hamitic inhabitants and settled there. Asiel's place in this genealogy testifies that his family held a prominent position within a tribe that otherwise has a modest role in the biblical writings.

keyEvents.title: Mentioned in the genealogy of Simeon
keyEvents.description: Asiel is listed as part of the genealogy of the tribe of Simeon in 1 Chronicles, in the line Asiel → Serajah → Josibjah → Jehu. He is counted among the prominent ancestors of Simeonite leaders.

keyEvents.title: Descendants' Search for Grazing Land
keyEvents.description: Asiel's descendants were among the named Simeonite leaders who went out to seek grazing land for their flocks. They found lush and spacious pasture areas in the region near Gedor.

keyEvents.title: Expansion of the Simeonites under King Hezekiah
keyEvents.description: During the reign of King Hezekiah, Simeonite leaders, including descendants of Asiel, went to the region near Gedor and drove out the Hamitic inhabitants there. Some Simeonites also went to Mount Seir and struck down the remaining Amalekites.

versions.summary: Asiel was a patriarch in the tribe of Simeon, mentioned in 1 Chronicles. He is known as the grandfather or ancestor of Jehu, and his descendants were among those who sought grazing land and settled in new areas during the time of King Hezekiah.
versions.title: Simeonite Patriarch
versions.reason: [minor] The title 'Simeonite Patriarch' is functional but could be slightly more descriptive to distinguish Asiel from other Simeonite patriarchs.; [major] Asiel is not described as a 'leader' in the biblical text. He is mentioned only as part of a genealogy. The role 'patriarch' would be more accurate. It is his descendants who are described as leaders or heads.; [minor] In 1 Chr 4:35, the lineage is Asiel → Seraja → Josibja → Jehu. The child 'Seraja-Simeonite' appears correct, but the ID should be verified against actual data.; [minor] The last three events actually concern Asiel's descendants, not Asiel himself. It is acceptable to include them for context, but the descriptions should clarify that these are actions of his descendants, not direct actions by Asiel.; [major] Footnotes are missing. A biblical person profile should have at least one footnote covering linguistic, historical, or theological details, such as the meaning of the name, the situation of the Simeonites, or the historical context during Hezekiah.; [minor] The lifespan 'c. 800–700 BC' is a reasonable estimate given that his descendants were active during Hezekiah's reign (c. 715–686 BC), but it is highly uncertain. Depending on how many generations separated Asiel from the time of Hezekiah, the dating could be adjusted.; [minor] Verse 41 mentions the destruction of the tent-dwellers/Hamites, but the event 'Expansion of the Simeonites under Hezekiah' refers mainly to the context in verses 38–41. There is some overlap between events 2, 3, and 4.

versions.summary: Asiel was a patriarch in the tribe of Simeon, mentioned in the genealogy of 1 Chronicles (1 Chron 4:35). He is listed as an ancestor in the line Asiel → Serajah → Josibiah → Jehu. Although little is known about Asiel personally, his descendants were among the Simeonite leaders who, during the reign of King Hezekiah (ca. 715–686 B.C.E.), sought new grazing lands and expanded Simeonite territory by settling in the Gedor valley and defeating the Hamitic inhabitants there.

versions.reason: [minor] The summary is well-written and informative, but resembles version 1 in the opening ('Asiel was an ancestor in the tribe of Simeon, mentioned in...'). Rephrasing the opening could provide more variety and avoid repetition.; [minor] The event 'The descendants' search for grazing land' overlaps significantly with the third event concerning the expansion of the Simeonites under Hezekiah. Verses 38–40 deal with named heads of families and their search for grazing land, while verses 41–43 concern the actual settlement. It may be appropriate to combine these or clarify the difference more clearly.; [minor] The footnote refers to '1 Chr 4:41' in parentheses, which is correct, but the phrasing 'ḥerem-like language' might be somewhat technical for a broader readership. versions.summary: In the genealogies of the tribe of Simeon in First Chronicles (1 Chr 4:35), Asiel is mentioned as one of the prominent ancestors in the line Asiel → Seraja → Josibja → Jehu. Although no independent account of Asiel's life has been preserved, his descendants played an important role among the Simeonite leaders. During the reign of King Hezekiah (ca. 715–686 BC), these leaders sought new grazing lands and expanded the territory of the Simeonites by going to the valley of Gedor, where they drove out the Hamitic inhabitants and settled there. Asiel's place in the genealogy testifies that his family belonged to the leading families in a tribe otherwise little mentioned in the biblical writings.

versions.reason: [minor] The description mentions the 'Valley of Gedor', but the text in 1 Chr 4:39 uses the phrasing 'the entrance to Gedor' or 'east of the valley', depending on translation. 'Valley of Gedor' is a simplification that may be imprecise. Consider a more neutral formulation such as 'the area near Gedor'.; [minor] The description notes that some went to 'Mount Seir', but this is referenced in verses 42–43, not directly linked to Asiel himself. It is fine to include, but please clarify that this applies to the Simeonites generally, not necessarily Asiel's direct descendants.; [minor] The summary is well written and informative, but the phrasing 'Valley of Gedor' should be adjusted to something more neutral like 'the area near Gedor' to avoid committing to one specific reading of the base text.

footnotes.text: The name Asiel (עֲשִׂיאֵל) likely means 'God has created' or 'created by God,' from the Hebrew roots עשׂה (asah, 'to do/create') and אֵל (El, 'God'). This theophoric name reflects a confession of God as Creator, similar to other biblical-Hebrew personal names such as Asael and Jaasiel.

The tribe of Simeon had a relatively small territory within Judah's inheritance (Josh 19:1–9). Over time, the Simeonites were largely absorbed into Judah, which may explain why they sought new grazing lands. The genealogies in Chronicles preserve the memory of Simeonite clans that might otherwise have been forgotten.

The expansion into the Gedor area under King Hezekiah (ca. 715–686 B.C.E.) can be seen in connection with Hezekiah's general strengthening of Judah following Assyrian pressure. Some scholars have suggested that 'Gedor' may be a mistranscription of 'Gerar' in the Septuagint, which would place the expansion in the Negev region toward the Egyptian border.

The account that the Simeonites drove out and destroyed the Hamitic inhabitants (1 Chron 4:41) uses language reminiscent of ḥerem – the complete consecration to destruction known from conquest narratives. This term is linked to the concept of holy war in the Old Testament.

The genealogies in Chronicles, especially for smaller tribes like Simeon, are believed to be based on older tribal lists and archives. These lists serve both a genealogical and a geographical function, linking clans to specific territories and thereby legitimizing territorial claims.

In rabbinic tradition, the tribe of Simeon is often associated with poverty and scattered settlement, which aligns with Jacob's prophetic words in Gen 49:7 that Simeon and Levi should be 'scattered in Israel.' The Chronicler's account of Simeonite expansion under Hezekiah can be understood as a partial reversal of this scattering.
